title: Promoting a More Candid Discussion in Real Time
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post tackles the moment when a normally engaged team goes quiet on a hard topic and the leader's pushing only makes it worse. The author's remedy is to pause the discussion and shift to brainstorming the pros and cons of the issue. Because every topic has something for both sides of the ledger, listing them gives the leader material to push against and restores the conditions for advocacy. For large groups, a red team and blue team variation has subgroups generate only positives or only negatives before reporting back, which may take 10 to 20 minutes. The claim is that getting people talking and generating views primes them to speak frankly. The post ends with the metaphor that you must drill a well before you can strike discussion oil.
points: Pressing harder for candor tends to backfire, so the leader should change the activity rather than raise the pressure.
A quick pros and cons ledger gives a hesitant team neutral material to argue with.
The red team and blue team split lets subgroups voice one side each, lowering the personal risk of speaking.
The author accepts a 10 to 20 minute investment as worthwhile for the candor it produces.
Simple, back-to-basics tools like brainstorming are presented as solutions to difficult dynamics.
quotes: Taking just a few minutes to quickly generate all the pros and cons of the issue, decision, or topic can reestablish the grounds for advocacy.

In every topic or issue, a leader can find something for the ledger of pros and cons. Once the pluses and minuses have been listed, the leader simply needs to push against any of them to foment more candid discussion.

With large groups and teams, when time allows, breaking into smaller units and having them brainstorm the pros and cons on their own before reporting back in the larger group is a red team/blue team variation that works just as well, sometimes even better.
Perhaps nothing is more critical for teams than to discuss challenging problems, decisions, and issues boldly and with the conviction created by open advocacy and debate.
Priming a team hesitant to engage fully is sometimes as easy as getting them to first brainstorm before taking up the issue again. The only way to strike discussion oil is to first drill a well.
